Pipette: Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming for Robust LLM Agents

Lipeng He1, Yihan Wang1🖂, Jiawen Zhang2, N. Asokan13 ††thanks: 🖂 Yihan Wang is the corresponding author. Affiliation: 1University of Waterloo, 2Zhejiang University, 3KTH Royal Institute of Technology Affiliation: lipeng.he@uwaterloo.ca, yihan.wang@uwaterloo.ca, kevinzh@zju.edu.cn, asokan@acm.org
Abstract

Large language model (LLM) agents routinely interact with untrusted external data, exposing them to indirect prompt injection (IPI) attacks that hijack agents into executing attacker-chosen tasks. To uncover these vulnerabilities at scale, automated red-teaming methods often leverage reinforcement learning (RL) to generate attacks that achieve high attack success rates (ASR). Model developers use the attacks discovered during internal red-teaming to harden agents through adversarial training before deployment, a collaborative offensive-defensive process known in cybersecurity as purple-teaming. However, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee robustness gains from subsequent adversarial training. Specifically, we find that two state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, suffer from mode collapse, repeatedly discovering similar attack strategies whose additional successes add no additional robustness improvements to adversarial training. To address this gap, we introduce Pipette, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that effectively converts red-teaming discoveries into defender robustness improvements. Pipette employs a dictionary learning-based reward that encourages broader coverage of attack strategies during red-teaming. It also integrates an on-policy adversarial training pipeline tailored to IPI defense, enabling agents to resist attacks while completing legitimate user tasks. Extensive evaluations across agentic benchmarks (AgentDojo and ASB) demonstrate that Pipette produces defenders that achieve near-zero attack success rates on static attacks and can withstand strong adaptive attacks, while maintaining benign task utility close to that of the undefended baseline.

I Introduction

Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that execute multi-step tasks, such as managing emails, querying databases, and invoking external APIs [1, 2]. To complete a user task specified by a trusted user instruction, an LLM agent must process untrusted external data retrieved from third-party sources, including web pages, documents, and tool outputs. Because LLMs cannot reliably distinguish between user instructions and external data [3], an attacker can embed a malicious injected instruction inside external data to override the user instruction and redirect the agent toward an attacker-chosen injection task [4, 2, 5]. This vulnerability, known as indirect prompt injection (IPI), allows remote attackers to exfiltrate private data or trigger unauthorized actions [6].

To harden an LLM agent before deployment, model developers pair automated red-teaming, where a red-teamer probes the agent to discover successful prompt injections, with adversarial training on the discovered attacks so the agent learns to resist them (Figure 1) [7, 8]. Among automated red-teaming methods [9], reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as the state-of-the-art approach for prompt injection [10, 11, 12]. Instead of manually crafting prompts or optimizing individual attack strings one input at a time [13, 14], RL trains a generative red-teaming policy to synthesize attacks at scale across diverse tasks. Leading RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer [11] and PISmith [12], achieve high attack success rates (ASR), defined as the fraction of test inputs on which the agent executes the injection task, even against models hardened with prior defenses [15].

Despite the effectiveness of these methods as offensive stress tests, we show that achieving high ASR during red-teaming does not guarantee strong robustness after adversarial training. For instance, PISmith achieves higher train-time ASR than RL-Hammer on Qwen3-4B (68.75%68.75\% versus 33.39%33.39\%), yet yields a less robust agent after RL-based adversarial training (47.5%47.5\% versus 27.5%27.5\% ASR under the strongest of three unseen attacks, §III). We attribute this gap in part to an objective mismatch. Prior work on jailbreak defenses shows that robustness to unseen attacks depends on the variety of training attacks and not only on their number [16, 17], yet existing RL-based red-teaming methods optimize their policy primarily to maximize attack success. Such an objective can lead to mode collapse, a failure in which the policy converges to a narrow set of outputs that repeatedly exploit the same vulnerability [18, 16]. Specifically, once the red-teaming policy discovers a single effective attack strategy, a way of overriding the user instruction such as claiming that the user task is already complete, it tends to reuse that strategy across rollouts to collect high reward. To mitigate mode collapse, PISmith [12] and RL-Hammer [11] regularize the red-teaming policy with token-level entropy bonuses or embedding distance rewards. However, because these regularizers measure surface-level text differences rather than how the attack overrides the user instruction, the red-teaming policy can engage in reward hacking by rephrasing sentences or inserting unrelated text while relying on the same attack strategy. As a result, training an agent on thousands of rephrased versions of one attack strategy may patch only a single vulnerability and leave the agent exposed to unseen attacks at deployment.

Even when red-teaming uncovers distinct attacks, converting those discoveries into a practical defense is a second challenge. A useful prompt injection defense requires preserving benign utility on clean inputs and utility under attack when external data is contaminated [2]. Unlike jailbreak attacks [19], where the user is the attacker and the agent can refuse the harmful request, an agent under IPI must ignore the injected instruction inside external data while still using the surrounding data to complete the benign user instruction. Yet standard RL defenses [20] train the agent with trajectory-level, outcome-based rewards that assign a single scalar score to the entire trajectory based on whether the task succeeded or failed. Because such a score cannot identify which tokens caused the failure [21], agents trained with these rewards can learn to abort execution or refuse the user whenever external data appears suspicious, and thus sacrifice task completion for lower ASR.

To address both challenges, we introduce Pipette, a unified prompt injection purple-teaming framework that coordinates red-teaming and adversarial training toward a single objective of maximizing the hardened agent’s robustness. First, to mitigate mode collapse, Pipette guides the red-teaming policy with a dictionary learning-based reward. We decompose generated attacks into a sparse dictionary of reusable components that capture distinct attack strategies, and reward the red-teaming policy when a successful attack cannot be explained by previously discovered components. Second, to preserve benign utility during adversarial training, Pipette trains the agent on the collected attacks by combining reasoning-guided RL with token-level on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) [22, 21]. By assigning credit to individual tokens rather than relying solely on trajectory-level outcome rewards, Pipette aims to suppress reasoning and action tokens driven by the injected instruction while reinforcing tokens needed for the user task.

We evaluate Pipette on two standard IPI benchmarks under static and iterative-adaptive attacks, and summarize our contributions as follows:

  • •

    We show empirically that maximizing ASR or surface-level text diversity in state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods [11, 12] does not prevent mode collapse at the strategy level, which likely limits the robustness gains of subsequent adversarial training (§III-B and §IV-A).

  • •

    We design a dictionary learning-based strategy coverage reward that guides the red-teaming policy to discover new attack strategies rather than surface-level wording variations (§IV-B).

  • •

    We pair our red-teaming stage with an on-policy adversarial training pipeline using token-level self-distillation to preserve benign utility while resisting injected instructions (§IV-C).

  • •

    We show on two benchmarks that Pipette compares favorably with existing red-teaming and defense baselines, with ASR under iterative-adaptive attacks on AgentDojo ranging from 0%0\% to 10%10\% across the three models tested and benign utility remaining close to that of the undefended policies on all four models (§V, Appendix B).

II Background

II-A LLM-based Agent Workflow

We model an LLM agent as an agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta}, parameterized by weights θ\theta, that interleaves text generation with tool execution [2, 23]. At the start of an episode, πθ\pi_{\theta} receives a trusted system prompt ss and a trusted user task tut_{u}, and then acts over steps t=1,…,Tt=1,\ldots,T. At step tt, πθ\pi_{\theta} conditions on a clean context

Ht=(s,tu,a1:t−1,o1:t−1),H_{t}=\bigl(s,\;t_{u},\;a_{1:t-1},\;o_{1:t-1}\bigr), (1)

where a1:t−1a_{1:t-1} and o1:t−1o_{1:t-1} are the actions and observations from steps 11 through t−1t-1, with H1=(s,tu)H_{1}=(s,t_{u}). Given HtH_{t}, πθ\pi_{\theta} samples an action

at∼πθ(⋅∣Ht),at=(ρt,ct),a_{t}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid H_{t}),\qquad a_{t}=(\rho_{t},c_{t}), (2)

where ρt\rho_{t} is natural-language reasoning or response text and ctc_{t} is a set of tool calls. When ct≠∅c_{t}\neq\emptyset, the tool calls return a clean observation oto_{t} that extends the context to Ht+1H_{t+1} with external data such as retrieved documents, emails, web pages, or API responses. Execution ends at step TT when cT=∅c_{T}=\emptyset, producing a completed clean trajectory τ=(s,tu,a1:T,o1:T−1)\tau=(s,t_{u},a_{1:T},o_{1:T-1}). We refer to the observation sequence {ot}t=1T−1\{o_{t}\}_{t=1}^{T-1} as the data channel. Unlike the trusted system prompt ss and user task tut_{u}, the data channel comes from external sources and is therefore untrusted.

II-B Indirect Prompt Injection

An external attacker 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can exploit the untrusted data channel through an indirect prompt injection (IPI) attack by embedding a malicious injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, or injection for short, into an external data source [4, 2]. When πθ\pi_{\theta} retrieves that source at step tt, the clean observation oto_{t} is replaced by a contaminated observation ot′o^{\prime}_{t} carrying dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, which contaminates every subsequent context Hk′H^{\prime}_{k} (k>tk>t) and induces an attacked trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime}. The injection string instructs πθ\pi_{\theta} to execute an injection task tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} that differs from tut_{u}. Let Φtadv​(⋅)∈{0,1}\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\cdot)\in\{0,1\} and Φtu​(⋅)∈{0,1}\Phi_{t_{u}}(\cdot)\in\{0,1\} denote binary predicates over completed trajectories that equal 11 when the injection task and user task are satisfied, respectively. On an attacked trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime}, the attack succeeds when Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1, and the user task succeeds when Φtu​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})=1. Over a set of attacked tasks, the fraction of attacked trajectories with Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1 is the attack success rate (ASR).

IPI differs from jailbreak attacks [19] in who controls the input. In a jailbreak attack, the user is 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} and tut_{u} itself is harmful, so πθ\pi_{\theta} only needs to refuse tut_{u}. In an IPI attack, however, the user task tut_{u} is benign and dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} arrives inside ot′o^{\prime}_{t} alongside benign external data that πθ\pi_{\theta} must read to finish tut_{u}. Halting before an unauthorized action can prevent it (Φtadv​(τ′)=0\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=0) while leaving the user task unfinished (Φtu​(τ′)=0\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})=0). To meet both goals, the agent must ignore dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} while retaining the benign data around it.

II-C Red-Teaming for Adversarial Training

To improve robustness against prompt injections without failing tut_{u}, a defender 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} can harden an initial base policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} into πθ\pi_{\theta} offline prior to deployment through adversarial training [24], which updates the model weights on contaminated contexts Ht′H^{\prime}_{t} carrying injection strings dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} so that πθ\pi_{\theta} learns to ignore dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} and complete tut_{u}. Prior IPI defenses instantiate adversarial training with several objectives on contaminated contexts: StruQ [3] uses supervised fine-tuning (SFT) to maximize the log-likelihood of clean reference actions; SecAlign [25] and Meta-SecAlign [15] use preference optimization to favor user-aligned responses over hijacked responses; SecOPD [21] uses on-policy distillation from a teacher model conditioned on clean observations; and RL-based adversarial training [20] rewards rollouts that complete tut_{u} without executing tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}. While StruQ, SecAlign, and Meta-SecAlign construct contaminated contexts using templated or hand-designed injection strings, hardening πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} against stronger attacks requires exposing it to a broader set of injection strings that bypass its safeguards across diverse tasks. Manually crafting such injections does not scale, so it is common practice for both industry [26, 7, 8, 27] and prior works [28, 29, 16] to pair automated red-teaming with adversarial training: 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} first runs an automated red-teamer offline against πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} to discover injection strings satisfying Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1, and then updates θ0\theta_{0} on them via adversarial training to obtain πθ\pi_{\theta}.

RL-based red-teaming is a commonly used method for generating these training injections at scale [11, 12, 8]. Instead of optimizing a separate injection string from scratch for each task, RL trains a generative red-teaming policy πϕ\pi_{\phi}, parameterized by ϕ\phi, offline across a training task set. Training a shared policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} amortizes exploration across tasks to produce thousands of successful injection strings at high ASR, and allows 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} to initialize πϕ\pi_{\phi} directly from πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} without requiring a stronger external model. Specifically, state-of-the-art RL-based red-teaming methods, RL-Hammer and PISmith, optimize πϕ\pi_{\phi} with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [30]. For each injection task tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}, GRPO samples a group of GG candidate injection strings from πϕ(⋅∣tadv)\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid t_{\mathrm{adv}}). Placing each candidate dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} into πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}’s data channel produces an attacked trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime} and a binary attack reward

ratk=Φtadv​(τ′).r_{\mathrm{atk}}=\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime}). (3)

GRPO normalizes ratkr_{\mathrm{atk}} using the group mean μatk\mu_{\mathrm{atk}} and standard deviation σatk\sigma_{\mathrm{atk}} to compute the advantage

A=ratk−μatkσatk,A=\frac{r_{\mathrm{atk}}-\mu_{\mathrm{atk}}}{\sigma_{\mathrm{atk}}}, (4)

and updates ϕ\phi to increase the probability of candidates with A>0A>0 while decreasing those with A<0A<0.

Reinforcing whichever candidates achieve A>0A>0 within each group can cause standard GRPO to converge to a narrow, repetitive set of successful injection strings [11, 12]. Recent RL-based red-teaming methods counter this repetition by regularizing surface text differences. RL-Hammer [11] studies auxiliary diversity rewards based on the pairwise BLEU score or the embedding distance between candidate injection strings generated by πϕ\pi_{\phi}, whereas PISmith [12] adds adaptive token-level entropy regularization and dynamic advantage weighting to the GRPO update. However, as we discuss in §III, regularizing token entropy or pairwise text distance over full injection strings does not necessarily enforce coverage of distinct attack strategies, the ways an injection string overrides tut_{u} (such as claiming that tut_{u} is already finished or framing tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} as workflow metadata). Instead, πϕ\pi_{\phi} can satisfy these surface regularizers through wording changes while repeatedly exploiting a single vulnerability [11].

II-D Adversary Model

Attacker’s goal and capabilities. At inference time, 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} aims to induce an attacked trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime} satisfying Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1 while the deployed agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta} executes a benign user task tut_{u}. 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can replace selected clean observations oto_{t} in the data channel with contaminated observations ot′o^{\prime}_{t} that embed dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} alongside the original data, yet cannot modify the system prompt ss, the user task tut_{u}, past actions a1:t−1a_{1:t-1}, the model weights θ\theta, or the execution environment [4, 3, 25].

We do not assume the defense is kept secret; rather, 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} knows the agent’s architecture, input format, and defense mechanism, acting as a defense-adaptive11 1 Prior ML literature uses the term “adaptive” to refer to defense-aware attackers while the security community uses the same term to refer to attackers who refine their attack by repeatedly interacting with the target. To avoid ambiguity, we use more precise terms, “defense-adaptive” and “iterative-adaptive” (respectively) to distinguish between these two types. attacker [31, 32]. 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} can also query the deployed agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta} repeatedly at inference time and observe the resulting trajectories τ′\tau^{\prime} and task outcomes. However, agent execution alternates between text generation and non-differentiable tool calls, so gradient-based token optimization designed for single-turn inputs [19] does not directly apply, and we restrict our evaluation to attacks that require no gradients [10]. Following established evaluation guidelines [31, 32, 10], we evaluate two classes of attacks at inference time:

  • •

    Static. Places pre-written injection strings dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} into the data channel in a single pass without querying πθ\pi_{\theta} or adapting to its outputs [4, 2, 33].

  • •

    Iterative-adaptive.1 Queries πθ\pi_{\theta} online in a live loop at inference time on each target task, inserting candidate injection strings dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, observing the resulting trajectories τ′\tau^{\prime}, and updating dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} across attempts to maximize Φtadv​(τ′)\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime}) [34, 10].

Iterative-adaptive attacks update dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} across queries using either RL or LLM-guided search. RL-based attacks such as AutoInject [35] train an attacker policy online, from the feedback of the deployed πθ\pi_{\theta} on the task under attack. Although both rely on RL, these online attacks differ from the red-teaming in §II-C, which 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} runs offline against πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} to collect injection strings for adversarial training. Search-based attacks instead use two auxiliary LLMs: an attacker LLM that rewrites candidate injection strings dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} based on prior trajectories τ′\tau^{\prime}, and a judge LLM that scores how close each τ′\tau^{\prime} comes to completing tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} [34, 36, 10]. Template-guided search such as Strategy [36] restricts the attacker LLM to a predefined list of rewrite rules. Open-ended search removes this restriction and lets the attacker LLM freely rewrite dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} over hundreds of online queries per task, which often achieves higher ASR. Among these attacks, we evaluate two open-ended searches: Tree of Attacks with Pruning (TAP) [34], which is widely used in practice [3, 36], and genetic search (Genetic) [10], which achieves state-of-the-art ASR across recent IPI defenses. TAP branches candidate rewrites in a tree and prunes low-scoring branches with the judge LLM, whereas Genetic evolves a MAP-Elites grid of candidates across generations without early pruning. Both can require hundreds of online rollouts and auxiliary LLM calls per task. This cost makes them strong inference-time stress tests on evaluation sets but impractical for generating thousands of injection strings across a training set, where RL-based red-teaming (§II-C) is used instead.

Defender’s goal and capabilities. Before deployment, the defender 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} (the model developer) hardens the base policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} into πθ\pi_{\theta} offline inside a controlled sandbox over a set of simulated task pairs 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}}. Each task pair specifies a user task tut_{u}, an injection task tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}, and the simulated tool environment in which the agent executes to produce trajectories τ\tau and τ′\tau^{\prime}. Within this sandbox, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} initializes the red-teaming policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} from πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} itself, has white-box access to the weights, evaluates Φtu\Phi_{t_{u}} and Φtadv\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}} on simulated trajectories, and knows the exact injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} placed in each contaminated observation ot′o^{\prime}_{t}.

At inference time, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} deploys πθ\pi_{\theta} to serve inference requests, and the sandbox assumptions are removed; πθ\pi_{\theta} does not control incoming observations in the data channel and does not know whether an observation oto_{t} is contaminated, where dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} appears, or which injection task tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} and attack method 𝖠𝖽𝗏\mathsf{Adv} uses. 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} aims to satisfy three requirements:

  • R1.

    Robustness. Under static or iterative-adaptive attacks, πθ\pi_{\theta} should not execute the injection task, Φtadv​(τ′)=0\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=0, minimizing ASR (§II-B).

  • R2.

    Utility under attack. Under attack, πθ\pi_{\theta} should still complete the user task, Φtu​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})=1. We measure this by utility under attack (UA), the fraction of attacked trajectories τ′\tau^{\prime} with Φtu​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})=1.

  • R3.

    Benign utility. On clean inputs where ot′=oto^{\prime}_{t}=o_{t} for all tt, πθ\pi_{\theta} should complete tut_{u} at a rate comparable to πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}. We measure this by benign utility (BU), the fraction of clean trajectories τ\tau with Φtu​(τ)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau)=1.

III Motivating Study and Problem Analysis

In cybersecurity, pairing offensive red-teaming with defensive blue-teaming, which here takes the form of adversarial training (§II-C), is called purple-teaming [37, 38]. This workflow implicitly assumes that a stronger red-teamer, which achieves higher ASR against the base policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}, uncovers more vulnerabilities, so that training on its discoveries produces a more robust policy πθ\pi_{\theta}. We formalize this workflow (Figure 1) in §III-A and examine the assumption in §III-B, along with the utility cost of adversarial training.

III-A Prompt Injection Purple-Teaming

Collecting successful injections via RL-based red-teaming. How the red-teaming policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} in §II-C is used depends on whether the goal is offensive evaluation or adversarial training. Studies that use RL-based red-teaming solely for offensive evaluation [11, 12] train πϕ\pi_{\phi} against πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}, discard the training trajectories, and evaluate only the final checkpoint of πϕ\pi_{\phi} on unseen tasks. In purple-teaming [28, 16, 7, 8], by contrast, all training steps of πϕ\pi_{\phi} over task pairs (tu,tadv)∈𝒟tasks(t_{u},t_{\mathrm{adv}})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} are used to collect injection strings that compromise πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}. Whenever a sampled candidate dadv∼πϕ(⋅∣tadv)d_{\mathrm{adv}}\sim\pi_{\phi}(\cdot\mid t_{\mathrm{adv}}) produces an attacked trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime} satisfying Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} adds the adversarial example (tu,tadv,dadv)(t_{u},t_{\mathrm{adv}},d_{\mathrm{adv}}) to the adversarial training dataset 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}:

𝒟train={(tu,tadv,dadv)|Φtadv​(τ′)=1}.\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}=\bigl\{\,(t_{u},t_{\mathrm{adv}},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\;\big|\;\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1\,\bigr\}. (5)

Adversarial training via SFT or RL. Given 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} updates πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} into an adversarially trained policy πθ\pi_{\theta} using either off-policy SFT [3, 16] or on-policy RL [20, 27]:

  • •

    Off-policy SFT. SFT trains πθ\pi_{\theta} to take the same actions on a contaminated context Ht′H^{\prime}_{t} that πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} takes on a clean context HtH_{t} [3]. For a user task tut_{u}, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} runs πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} on clean observations to record a clean trajectory τ=(s,tu,a1:T,o1:T−1)\tau=(s,t_{u},a_{1:T},o_{1:T-1}) with Φtu​(τ)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau)=1. For each (tu,tadv,dadv)∈𝒟train(t_{u},t_{\mathrm{adv}},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\in\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}, embedding dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} into the target observation yields contaminated contexts Ht′=(s,tu,a1:t−1,o1:t−1′)H^{\prime}_{t}=(s,t_{u},a_{1:t-1},o^{\prime}_{1:t-1}). SFT updates θ\theta to minimize the negative log-likelihood of the clean actions a1:Ta_{1:T} given the contaminated context Ht′H^{\prime}_{t},

    ℒSFT​(θ)=−𝔼(tu,tadv,dadv)∼𝒟train​[∑t=1Tlog⁡πθ​(at∣Ht′)],\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{SFT}}(\theta)=-\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(t_{u},t_{\mathrm{adv}},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\\ \sim\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}\end{subarray}}\!\left[\sum_{t=1}^{T}\log\pi_{\theta}(a_{t}\mid H^{\prime}_{t})\right], (6)

    and adds the same loss on clean trajectories from 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} as a utility retain set. This update is off-policy because the target actions a1:Ta_{1:T} come from πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} acting on HtH_{t} rather than from πθ\pi_{\theta} acting on Ht′H^{\prime}_{t}.

  • •

    On-policy RL. Instead of copying pre-recorded actions, on-policy RL uses GRPO [30] to sample trajectories directly from πθ\pi_{\theta} on tasks carrying dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} from 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}, mixed with clean retain tasks from 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} [27]. To reward both user task completion (R2) and robustness (R1) in §II-D, each attacked trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime} receives a binary defense reward:

    rdef​(τ′)=Φtu​(τ′)⋅(1−Φtadv​(τ′))∈{0,1},r_{\mathrm{def}}(\tau^{\prime})=\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\bigl(1-\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})\bigr)\in\{0,1\}, (7)

    which equals 11 when πθ\pi_{\theta} completes tut_{u} without executing tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}, and 00 otherwise; on clean trajectories τ\tau, rdef​(τ)=Φtu​(τ)r_{\mathrm{def}}(\tau)=\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau).

In this workflow, a red-teamer with higher ASR compromises more task pairs in 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} and typically builds a larger dataset 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} in Eq. 5. We next examine whether this larger dataset also yields a more robust and equally useful policy.

III-B Red-Teaming Success May Not Always Lead to Defender Improvements

Study setup. At inference time, a deployed policy πθ\pi_{\theta} encounters tools, user tasks, and attacks absent from training. To approximate this setting, we separate our training and evaluation benchmarks, as summarized in Table I. We run offline red-teaming and adversarial training on 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}}, which comprises 560560 task pairs from AgentDyn [39], a multi-step agentic benchmark. We then evaluate all trained policies πθ\pi_{\theta} on 4040 task pairs (Appendix C), 1010 from each of the four task suites of AgentDojo [2], whose user tasks are disjoint from those of AgentDyn. We test two base policies πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}: Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507 [40, 41], denoted Qwen3-4B, and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct [26], denoted Llama-8B. For red-teaming, we run RL-Hammer [11] and PISmith [12] on AgentDyn for 250250 steps with batch sizes of 128128 and 6464, matching the authors’ configurations, to construct 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}, and then train πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} on each dataset via SFT in Eq. 6 or RL in Eq. 7. On AgentDojo, we evaluate against three unseen attacks: ChatInject [33], a static attack that spoofs chat templates, and the iterative-adaptive attacks TAP [34] and Genetic [10], with Qwen3.5-4B as the attacker LLM and Qwen3-4B as the judge LLM.

Train-time ASR does not guarantee robustness. Table II reports each red-teamer’s train-time cumulative ASR, defined as the fraction of task pairs in 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} it compromised at least once, alongside the size of the resulting 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}}. PISmith reaches 68.75%68.75\% ASR on Qwen3-4B, compared with 33.39%33.39\% for RL-Hammer. The difference is smaller on Llama-8B, where the corresponding rates are 27.32%27.32\% and 25.18%25.18\%, but in both cases PISmith also supplies the defender with the larger training set.

If higher train-time ASR produced better training data, policies trained on PISmith would achieve lower inference-time ASR than policies trained on RL-Hammer. For each trained policy, Figure 2 shows its worst-case ASR, the highest of the three rates observed under ChatInject, TAP, and Genetic on the selected AgentDojo task pairs. Despite its higher train-time ASR, PISmith yields a higher worst-case ASR in three of the four settings. Under RL, switching from RL-Hammer to PISmith data raises this rate from 27.5%27.5\% to 47.5%47.5\% on Qwen3-4B and from 25.0%25.0\% to 27.5%27.5\% on Llama-8B. The same pattern holds under SFT on Llama-8B, where ASR rises from 15.0%15.0\% to 20.0%20.0\%. Only under SFT on Qwen3-4B does PISmith yield a lower worst-case ASR (12.5%12.5\% versus 15.0%15.0\%). Across the four settings, worst-case ASR ranges between 12.5%12.5\% and 47.5%47.5\%.

To understand why collecting more successful injection strings does not necessarily improve robustness, we examine the training objective of πϕ\pi_{\phi}. Prior work shows that maximizing attack reward in Eq. 3 only requires πϕ\pi_{\phi} to find one working attack strategy and apply it across tasks [18, 16]. Although PISmith and RL-Hammer include diversity regularizers (§II-C), neither regularizer measures whether dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} introduces a new attack strategy. Specifically, PISmith shrinks the coefficient of its token-level entropy bonus to a small base value when the group mean reward μatk\mu_{\mathrm{atk}} crosses a threshold [12], which relaxes exploration as soon as πϕ\pi_{\phi} finds a working attack strategy. Similarly, RL-Hammer’s diversity rewards compare lexical n-gram overlap (pairwise BLEU) or embedding distance over the full injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, and its authors report that πϕ\pi_{\phi} satisfies them by changing letter case and wording or by prepending irrelevant text while reusing the same attack strategy [11]. We therefore hypothesize that higher train-time ASR comes from applying the same few attack strategies across more tasks in 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}}, which leaves other attack strategies open when TAP and Genetic search for new injection strings at inference time [10, 17].

Adversarial training can degrade benign utility. Beyond robustness, a hardened policy must also preserve benign utility (R3). Adversarial training, however, is known to induce a trade-off between robustness and utility on clean inputs [42]. This trade-off has been observed both in jailbreak defenses, where safety tuning degrades performance on benign prompts [28, 43], and in IPI defenses [44, 21].

Table III shows a similar trade-off for the policies trained above, reporting their BU on the 9797 clean AgentDojo user tasks. Off-policy SFT reduces Qwen3-4B BU from 61.86%61.86\% to 49.48%49.48\% on RL-Hammer and 53.61%53.61\% on PISmith. A likely reason is that, although SFT supervises clean reference actions in contaminated contexts, the reference trajectory gives no feedback when πθ\pi_{\theta} deviates from it; if fine-tuning shifts πθ\pi_{\theta} toward refusing a task or aborting a tool call whenever a clean observation contains imperatively phrased text, BU drops [44, 21]. On-policy RL, on the other hand, does provide feedback on the actions πθ\pi_{\theta} chooses, rewarding it for completing tut_{u} on its own trajectories. On Qwen3-4B, this retains more BU than SFT on both training sets (54.64%54.64\% on RL-Hammer data and 60.82%60.82\% on PISmith data). However, switching to RL does not always recover clean-task performance. On Llama-8B, BU is 29.90%29.90\% after RL on RL-Hammer data versus 40.21%40.21\% for πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}, while worst-case ASR remains 25.0%25.0\% (Figure 2). One possible reason this gap persists is that Eq. 7 assigns a single binary reward rdef​(τ′)∈{0,1}r_{\mathrm{def}}(\tau^{\prime})\in\{0,1\} to the entire trajectory τ′\tau^{\prime}. An agent that ignores dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} but stops before finishing tut_{u} receives rdef​(τ′)=0r_{\mathrm{def}}(\tau^{\prime})=0, just as it would for executing tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}. Although the two failures call for different corrections, this score gives the agent no direct feedback about which tokens led to either outcome [22, 21].

IV Our Method

In §III, PISmith compromised more training tasks than RL-Hammer, yet training on its examples yielded a higher worst-case ASR in three of the four settings. If those additional successes came from reusing familiar strategies on new tasks, the collection could grow without exposing the defender to other ways of redirecting the agent (Remark 1). Since a familiar strategy can appear in an injection whose wording is new, we test this explanation by measuring how well the strategies represented in the collection explain unseen injections as the collection grows (§IV-A). In Pipette (Figure 3 and Algorithm 1), this measure also guides Pipette-Red (§IV-B) as it collects the examples on which Pipette-Blue trains the defender (§IV-C).

IV-A Revisiting Red-Teaming Objectives for Defense Improvements

From surface wording to strategy primitives. In §III-B, we hypothesized that RL-based red-teamers achieve high train-time ASR while leaving other vulnerabilities open because pairwise BLEU, sentence embeddings, and token entropy bonuses (§II-C) operate on raw injection strings dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} rather than on the attack strategies behind them. In particular, two injection strings can share almost no words yet use the same attack strategy to override tut_{u} [11, 17], because task-specific nouns such as email addresses or account numbers dominate full-string similarity. Conversely, a single injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} can combine several attack strategies in one text [17]. To test our hypothesis and guide red-teaming toward new vulnerabilities, we therefore need to remove noise such as task-specific nouns and decompose each injection string into reusable components that capture distinct attack strategies, which we call strategy primitives.

Prior work on jailbreak attacks shows that adversarial prompts can be broken down into recurring attack strategies using an LLM [17]. Adapting this decomposition to IPI, we pass each successful injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} to an LLM extractor that outputs one or more structured strategy records ψ⁡(dadv)\psi(d_{\mathrm{adv}}). Each record contains three fields: a short strategy name, the matched verbatim text in dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, and a task-agnostic explanation ee of how that text redirects the agent policy away from tut_{u}.

Across thousands of rollouts, raw strategy explanations {ej}j=1N\{e_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} still contain many near-duplicate descriptions of the same attack strategy, as well as descriptions that blend multiple strategies. To handle both, we apply sparse dictionary learning [45, 46, 17], which represents each explanation vector as a sparse linear combination of K≪NK\ll N shared strategy primitives. Using an embedding model ℰ\mathcal{E}, we map each explanation eje_{j} to an ℓ2\ell_{2}-normalized vector 𝐱j=ℰ⁡(ej)/‖ℰ⁡(ej)‖2∈ℝp\mathbf{x}_{j}=\mathcal{E}(e_{j})/\|\mathcal{E}(e_{j})\|_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} to form the explanation matrix 𝐗=[𝐱1,…,𝐱N]∈ℝp×N\mathbf{X}=[\mathbf{x}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{x}_{N}]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times N}. We then learn a strategy dictionary 𝐃=[𝐝1,…,𝐝K]∈ℝp×K\mathbf{D}=[\mathbf{d}_{1},\ldots,\mathbf{d}_{K}]\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times K} whose KK columns represent the strategy primitives, together with a sparse code matrix 𝚪∈ℝK×N\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times N}, by solving

min𝐃,𝚪⁡12​‖𝐗−𝐃​𝚪‖F2+α​‖𝚪‖1,1s.t.​‖𝐝k‖2≤1,\min_{\mathbf{D},\,\boldsymbol{\Gamma}}\;\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\|_{F}^{2}+\alpha\|\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\|_{1,1}\quad\text{s.t.}\;\;\|\mathbf{d}_{k}\|_{2}\leq 1, (8)

where ‖𝐗−𝐃​𝚪‖F2\|\mathbf{X}-\mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\|_{F}^{2} measures how well 𝐃\mathbf{D} reconstructs the vectors in 𝐗\mathbf{X}, and the ℓ1\ell_{1} penalty α​‖𝚪‖1,1\alpha\|\boldsymbol{\Gamma}\|_{1,1} with α>0\alpha>0 encourages each 𝐱j\mathbf{x}_{j} to use only a few columns of 𝐃\mathbf{D}.

Because each learned column 𝐝k∈ℝp\mathbf{d}_{k}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} is an unlabeled vector, we translate 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k} back into text by finding a sparse set of original records in 𝐗\mathbf{X} that reconstructs 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k}. Specifically, we solve a Basis Pursuit Denoising (BPDN) ℓ1\ell_{1}-regularized least-squares problem [47, 17]:

𝜷^=arg⁡min𝜷∈ℝN​12​‖𝐝k−𝐗​𝜷‖22+λ​‖𝜷‖1,\hat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in\mathbb{R}^{N}}\;\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{d}_{k}-\mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\beta}\|_{1}, (9)

where λ>0\lambda>0 controls the sparsity of 𝜷\boldsymbol{\beta} over the NN columns of 𝐗\mathbf{X}. Ranking the records in 𝐗\mathbf{X} by coefficient magnitude |β^j||\hat{\beta}_{j}| then selects the top strategy records for 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k}, from which an LLM writes a canonical name, description, and example realization for strategy primitive 𝐝k\mathbf{d}_{k}. Finally, near-duplicate primitives whose description embeddings have cosine similarity above a threshold are merged [17]. Two learned strategy primitives are shown below.

Measuring strategy coverage via explainability. A single injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} can combine multiple strategy primitives at once, such as pairing signal-based instruction override with task-framing instruction. Because matching dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} to a single column in 𝐃\mathbf{D} cannot capture a combination of primitives, we measure whether 𝐃\mathbf{D} covers a new injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} by decomposing each explanation e∈ψ⁡(dadv)e\in\psi(d_{\mathrm{adv}}) with normalized embedding 𝐱=ℰ⁡(e)/‖ℰ⁡(e)‖2\mathbf{x}=\mathcal{E}(e)/\|\mathcal{E}(e)\|_{2} into a sparse combination of columns in 𝐃\mathbf{D} via BPDN:

𝜸^=arg⁡min𝜸∈ℝK​12​‖𝐱−𝐃​𝜸‖22+λ​‖𝜸‖1.\hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}=\arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\gamma}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}}\;\frac{1}{2}\|\mathbf{x}-\mathbf{D}\boldsymbol{\gamma}\|_{2}^{2}+\lambda\|\boldsymbol{\gamma}\|_{1}. (10)

In the sparse code 𝜸^∈ℝK\hat{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\in\mathbb{R}^{K}, the largest magnitudes |γ^k||\hat{\gamma}_{k}| identify the strategy primitives in 𝐃\mathbf{D} that actively reconstruct 𝐱\mathbf{x}. Because vector reconstruction in embedding space can still assign partial weights to loosely related columns when dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} introduces an uncovered strategy, we retrieve the descriptions of the top strategy primitives in 𝐃\mathbf{D} ranked by |γ^k||\hat{\gamma}_{k}| and pass them, together with ψ⁡(dadv)\psi(d_{\mathrm{adv}}) and dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, to an LLM grader. The grader rates from 11 to 55 how completely those primitives explain how dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} redirects the agent policy. Rescaling this rating to [0,1][0,1] and averaging across the records in ψ⁡(dadv)\psi(d_{\mathrm{adv}}) gives the Explainability Score [17] ES⁡(𝐃,dadv)∈[0,1]\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\in[0,1]. Intuitively, changing filler words or punctuation activates the same primitives in 𝐃\mathbf{D} and yields ES⁡(𝐃,dadv)≈1\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\approx 1, whereas introducing an attack strategy absent from 𝐃\mathbf{D} yields ES⁡(𝐃,dadv)≈0\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\approx 0.

Testing strategy-level mode collapse in prior red-teamers. Using ES\mathrm{ES}, we test our hypothesis from §III-B on 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} collected by RL-Hammer and PISmith. We order the successful injection strings of each red-teamer by discovery time and divide them into equal intervals of 2525 RL steps, which we call dictionary iterations. For each iteration ℓ∈{1,…,9}\ell\in\{1,\ldots,9\}, we learn a cumulative dictionary 𝐃ℓ\mathbf{D}_{\ell} via Eqs. 8 and 9 on all successful injection strings up to that iteration, and compute the mean ES⁡(𝐃ℓ,dadv)\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D}_{\ell},d_{\mathrm{adv}}) on unseen ChatInject injection strings [33]. If a red-teamer kept uncovering attack strategies that unseen attacks also rely on, the cumulative dictionary 𝐃ℓ\mathbf{D}_{\ell} should explain the unseen ChatInject attacks increasingly well, and ES⁡(𝐃ℓ,dadv)\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D}_{\ell},d_{\mathrm{adv}}) should rise across iterations. In Figure 4, however, RL-Hammer plateaus near ES≈0.20\mathrm{ES}\approx 0.20 on Qwen3-4B and 0.350.35 on Llama-8B, while PISmith stagnates or drifts downward after the first two iterations, possibly because repeated strategies dominate the reconstruction loss in Eq. 8. By contrast, Pipette-Red (§IV-B), which rewards its own injection strings for low ES\mathrm{ES} during red-teaming to sustain exploration, later reaches higher ES\mathrm{ES} on the unseen attacks than both baselines (≈0.60\approx 0.60 on Qwen3-4B and 0.770.77 on Llama-8B).

IV-B Pipette-Red: Strategy-Guided Red-Teaming

Strategy coverage reward. In Eq. 3, πϕ\pi_{\phi} receives the same reward for repeating a known attack strategy as for discovering a new one, which likely contributes to the ES\mathrm{ES} plateau in Remark 3. To push πϕ\pi_{\phi} toward uncovered strategies, Pipette-Red (Figure 3, left) maintains a rolling strategy dictionary 𝐃ℓ∈ℝp×K\mathbf{D}_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{p\times K} over the red-teaming steps, which are divided into dictionary iterations ℓ≥1\ell\geq 1. As in §II-C, each of the GG candidates sampled for a task pair is rolled out against the frozen base policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}, and each rollout (dadv,τ′)(d_{\mathrm{adv}},\tau^{\prime}) receives three rewards forming the reward set 𝒞={atk,fmt,cov}\mathcal{C}=\{\mathrm{atk},\mathrm{fmt},\mathrm{cov}\}: the binary attack reward ratkr_{\mathrm{atk}} in Eq. 3, a binary format reward rfmt∈{0,1}r_{\mathrm{fmt}}\in\{0,1\} that checks for structured reasoning before dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} [11, 12], and a continuous strategy coverage reward rcov∈[0,1]r_{\mathrm{cov}}\in[0,1] [18]:

rcov=Φtadv​(τ′)⋅(1−ES⁡(𝐃ℓ,dadv)),r_{\mathrm{cov}}=\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})\cdot\bigl(1-\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D}_{\ell},d_{\mathrm{adv}})\bigr), (11)

where rcov=0r_{\mathrm{cov}}=0 before 𝐃1\mathbf{D}_{1} is built. Multiplying by Φtadv​(τ′)\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime}) rewards coverage only when dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} compromises πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}}, which keeps πϕ\pi_{\phi} from outputting broken text just to lower ES\mathrm{ES}.

Rolling dictionary updates. If 𝐃ℓ\mathbf{D}_{\ell} stayed fixed at 𝐃1\mathbf{D}_{1} throughout red-teaming, πϕ\pi_{\phi} could maximize Eq. 11 by finding a single successful and novel attack strategy absent from 𝐃1\mathbf{D}_{1} and repeating it [18, 29]. Conversely, fitting 𝐃ℓ+1\mathbf{D}_{\ell+1} only on the latest rollouts would forget earlier strategy primitives and let πϕ\pi_{\phi} cycle back to old strategies. Therefore, whenever a rollout achieves Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1, Pipette-Red adds (tu,tadv,dadv)(t_{u},t_{\mathrm{adv}},d_{\mathrm{adv}}) to 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and extracts ψ⁡(dadv)\psi(d_{\mathrm{adv}}). Then, every MM RL steps, it rebuilds 𝐃ℓ+1\mathbf{D}_{\ell+1} via Eqs. 8 and 9 using the strategy records retained from prior iterations, together with new records from 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} satisfying ES⁡(𝐃ℓ,dadv)<δ\mathrm{ES}(\mathbf{D}_{\ell},d_{\mathrm{adv}})<\delta. Filtering additions by the threshold δ\delta keeps duplicate strategies from dominating Eq. 8, while retaining prior records means that repeating an earlier strategy still yields high ES\mathrm{ES} and thus near-zero rcovr_{\mathrm{cov}}.

Red-teaming policy optimization. Updating ϕ\phi from the three rewards in 𝒞\mathcal{C} combines two binary rewards with a continuous reward in [0,1][0,1]. In standard GRPO (Eq. 4), summing multiple rewards before dividing by the group standard deviation can let high-variance binary rewards outweigh lower-variance continuous rewards and map different reward combinations to the same sum [48]. To preserve the signal from each reward i∈𝒞i\in\mathcal{C}, we normalize it separately across the GG rollouts before taking the weighted sum [48]:

Ai=ri−μiσi+ϵ,ART=∑i∈𝒞wi​Ai,A_{i}=\frac{r_{i}-\mu_{i}}{\sigma_{i}+\epsilon},\qquad A_{\mathrm{RT}}=\sum_{i\in\mathcal{C}}w_{i}A_{i}, (12)

where μi\mu_{i} and σi\sigma_{i} are the group mean and standard deviation of reward ii, ϵ>0\epsilon>0 avoids division by zero, and wi>0w_{i}>0 weights reward ii. We standardize ARTA_{\mathrm{RT}} across the mini-batch and update ϕ\phi using clipped GRPO with adaptive token-level entropy regularization [30, 12].

IV-C Pipette-Blue: On-Policy Defensive Training

After Pipette-Red produces 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} spanning diverse attack strategies, Pipette-Blue (Figure 3, right) trains the agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta} on 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} toward the three defense requirements R1 to R3 (§II-D).

Task-alignment reasoning and outcome-based RL. To learn generalizable defensive behavior during adversarial training, Pipette-Blue trains the agent policy πθ\pi_{\theta} to separate untrusted data from instructions through explicit reasoning before acting. Prior work on jailbreak defense shows that training a model to reason over a fixed set of safety policies before responding improves generalization to unseen attacks [49]. Following this approach, Pipette-Blue trains πθ\pi_{\theta} to inspect the last observation ot−1o_{t-1} in its reasoning ρt\rho_{t} before emitting tool calls ctc_{t} (§II-A). This reasoning performs two checks [4, 50]: C1, identify whether ot−1o_{t-1} contains any instruction or attempt to redirect the task, and C2, verify that every planned tool call in ctc_{t} serves a goal authorized by the trusted user task tut_{u}. Under C2, observations may supply the data for that goal but cannot authorize a new one.

To establish this reasoning format without distilling from a larger model, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} prompts the base policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} to generate demonstrations whose reasoning ρt\rho_{t} follows C1 and C2. For this SFT warm-up, we use tasks in 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} and a weaker subset of AgentDojo’s built-in static attacks, which we exclude from evaluation. After the warm-up, Pipette-Blue trains πθ\pi_{\theta} with on-policy RL on attacked tasks from 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} and clean tasks from 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}}. Each of the GG rollouts in a group receives the outcome-based defense reward rdefr_{\mathrm{def}} in Eq. 7 and a chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning reward rCoT∈[0,1]r_{\mathrm{CoT}}\in[0,1]. To compute the latter, an LLM judge checks C1 and C2 in ρt\rho_{t} at each step and averages the binary results over the trajectory. We normalize and combine both rewards as in Eq. 12 to obtain the trajectory-level advantage AtrajA_{\mathrm{traj}}.

Contrastive token-level reward. To address the utility degradation observed in §III-B, where supervising multi-step rollouts solely with the outcome-based reward rdefr_{\mathrm{def}} can push πθ\pi_{\theta} toward overly cautious refusals, Pipette-Blue uses a token-level reward. To assign credit to individual tokens, we use the difference in information available at inference time versus offline training (§II-D). Intuitively, an IPI attack succeeds when πθ\pi_{\theta} is confused about the provenance of malicious instructions embedded in ot−1′o^{\prime}_{t-1}. If a user explicitly identified dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} and instructed the agent to ignore it, even the base policy πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} could often follow this directive and complete tut_{u} safely. At inference time, however, πθ\pi_{\theta} acts autonomously on behalf of the user, so no such guidance is available. During offline adversarial training, in contrast, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} has access to the exact injection string dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} placed in Ht′H^{\prime}_{t}. Before πθ\pi_{\theta} generates its reasoning and tool calls, 𝖣𝖾𝖿\mathsf{Def} can therefore add a privileged safe prefix z+z^{+} after Ht′H^{\prime}_{t} that instructs the agent to ignore dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} received from the tool output. Following on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) [22, 51], as πθ\pi_{\theta} samples an unprefixed on-policy action at=(y1,…,yL)∼πθ(⋅∣Ht′)a_{t}=(y_{1},\ldots,y_{L})\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid H^{\prime}_{t}), we query πθ\pi_{\theta} on the same tokens conditioned on (Ht′,z+)(H^{\prime}_{t},z^{+}) to supervise the unprefixed policy πθ​(yj∣Ht′,y<j)\pi_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid H^{\prime}_{t},y_{<j}) toward the safe target distribution πθ​(yj∣Ht′,z+,y<j)\pi_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid H^{\prime}_{t},z^{+},y_{<j}).

The positive prefix z+z^{+} changes the prompt’s form as well as its instruction. Maximizing agreement with this prefix alone could therefore reward a change in formatting, such as closing the reasoning block before the agent has worked through the task. To reduce this shared prefix effect, we pair z+z^{+} with a matched unsafe prefix z−z^{-} that instead instructs the agent to follow dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}. At each step tt where Ht′H^{\prime}_{t} contains dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}, we score the unprefixed tokens without taking gradients through either scoring pass. For each yjy_{j}, we compute the log-probability ratio

rtok​(yj)=log⁡πθ​(yj∣Ht′,z+,y<j)πθ​(yj∣Ht′,z−,y<j),r_{\mathrm{tok}}(y_{j})=\log\frac{\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{j}\mid H^{\prime}_{t},z^{+},y_{<j}\bigr)}{\pi_{\theta}\bigl(y_{j}\mid H^{\prime}_{t},z^{-},y_{<j}\bigr)}, (13)

and add its centered, clipped value to the trajectory-level advantage AtrajA_{\mathrm{traj}} to obtain

Atok​(yj)=Atraj+wtok​clip​(rtok​(yj)−b,−κ,κ),A_{\mathrm{tok}}(y_{j})=A_{\mathrm{traj}}+w_{\mathrm{tok}}\,\mathrm{clip}\bigl(r_{\mathrm{tok}}(y_{j})-b,\;-\kappa,\;\kappa\bigr), (14)

where bb is the batch mean of rtokr_{\mathrm{tok}}, wtok>0w_{\mathrm{tok}}>0 is the token weight, κ>0\kappa>0 is the clipping bound, and the second term is zero on clean tasks and steps before dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} enters Ht′H^{\prime}_{t}. Both z+z^{+} and z−z^{-} quote the same dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} in a common format (Appendix E), so the ratio is designed to reduce sensitivity to that shared formatting. A positive rtok​(yj)r_{\mathrm{tok}}(y_{j}) means that the token was more likely when the policy was told to ignore the injection and continue tut_{u}, while a negative value means it was more likely when the policy was told to carry out tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}. While SecOPD [21] distills from a teacher conditioned on the clean context HtH_{t} with dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} removed, scoring tokens via z+z^{+} and z−z^{-} directly on Ht′H^{\prime}_{t} lets πθ\pi_{\theta} learn to recognize and ignore dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} while extracting the surrounding benign data needed for tut_{u}.

V Experiments

To determine what the defender gains from a better training set (§III), we vary the collection and the training procedure separately (§V-B). We then evaluate the trained agent under iterative-adaptive and static attacks (R1, §V-C and §V-D). Since a refusal can also prevent an injection, we assess utility alongside robustness (R2 and R3, §V-E) and examine how Pipette-Blue’s supervision affects both in an ablation (§V-F).

V-A Experimental Setup

Models and benchmarks. We evaluate four open-weight models spanning three model families from 4B to 27B parameters: Qwen3-4B and Llama-8B from §III-B, GPT-OSS-20B [52], and Qwen3.6-27B [53]. Across all models, both stages of Pipette run offline exclusively on AgentDyn tasks [39]. At inference time, we evaluate the trained policies on two unseen multi-step benchmarks: AgentDojo [2], covering the Workspace, Slack, Travel, and Banking suites, and Agent Security Bench (ASB) [54]. No user task tut_{u} or injection task tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} of AgentDojo or ASB appears in training.

Defense baselines and evaluation protocol. In §V-B, we first evaluate the two stages of our framework individually: Pipette-Red (§IV-B) paired with RL or SFT adversarial training (§III-A), and Pipette-Blue (§IV-C) compared against RL and SFT on the dataset 𝒟train\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{train}} collected by Pipette-Red. In §V-C through §V-E, we compare the complete Pipette against two categories of prior IPI defenses:

  • •

    Training-based defenses update the policy weights θ\theta offline via adversarial training prior to deployment and add no external components at inference time, including Meta-SecAlign [15], SecOPD [21], and Instruction Hierarchy [55], which is natively trained into GPT-OSS-20B [52].

  • •

    Non-training-based defenses leave the policy weights θ\theta unchanged and place inference-time safeguards around the agent policy, including prompt boundary defenses (Spotlighting [56], Sandwiching [57]), external input classifiers (PromptGuard [58], PIGuard [44]), canary detection (DataSentinel [59]), masked re-execution (MELON [23]), and system-level control- and data-flow isolation (CaMeL [60]).

The training-based baselines are released for different models, so we use the authors’ checkpoints on their native models: Meta-SecAlign on Llama-8B, SecOPD on Qwen3.6-27B, and the native Instruction Hierarchy in GPT-OSS-20B. Since prior studies already report near-zero ASR for trained defenses on static attacks [15, 21], we focus the main comparison on iterative-adaptive attacks on AgentDojo (§V-C) and give the static results in Appendix B. We evaluate the non-training-based defenses on Qwen3-4B and Llama-8B under the built-in attacks of AgentDojo and ASB (§V-D). We exclude the weaker AgentDojo attacks used to initialize the output formats of πϕ\pi_{\phi} and πθ\pi_{\theta}, such as Direct and SystemMsg (§IV-C, Appendix D).

Attacks and metrics. Static evaluations on AgentDojo cover IgnorePrev [61], InjecAgent [62], ImportantMsgs [2], ToolKnow [2], and ChatInject [33]; those on ASB cover Naive, Escape, Ignore, Completion, and Combined [4, 54]. Iterative-adaptive evaluations use the two search-based attacks from §II-D, TAP [34] (up to 250250 attempts per task pair) and Genetic [10] (up to 248248 attempts per task pair), both with Qwen3.5-4B as the attacker LLM and Qwen3-4B as the judge LLM. Following §III-B, we run them on the same AgentDojo task pairs spanning all four suites (Appendix C). We report ASR, UA, and BU (§II-D); implementation details and prompts are in Appendices D and E.

V-B Pipette Achieves Robustness Improvements While Preserving Utility

We retain the setup of §III-B so that the changes in robustness and utility can be compared directly with the findings in Remarks 1 and 2.

Pipette-Red converts red-teaming discovery into lower inference-time ASR. Figure 5 plots train-time cumulative ASR on AgentDyn against worst-case inference-time ASR on AgentDojo across red-teaming methods and adversarial training algorithms. An effective red-teamer should occupy the bottom-right corner, combining high train-time ASR with low inference-time ASR after adversarial training. As observed in §III-B, moving from RL-Hammer to PISmith shifts the red-teamer rightward toward higher train-time cumulative ASR but, in three of the four settings, also upward toward higher worst-case inference-time ASR. In contrast, replacing baseline red-teaming with Pipette-Red moves all trained policies toward the bottom-right corner. Pipette-Red reaches the highest train-time cumulative ASR on both models (70.54%70.54\% with 8,2998{,}299 strings on Qwen3-4B, and 41.07%41.07\% with 2,1122{,}112 on Llama-8B). At the same time, training on its dataset yields the lowest worst-case inference-time ASR in all four settings, namely 20.0%20.0\% under RL and 2.5%2.5\% under SFT on Qwen3-4B, and 10.0%10.0\% under RL and 5.0%5.0\% under SFT on Llama-8B. These gains are consistent with the higher coverage of unseen ChatInject attacks in Figure 4, although the red-teamers also differ in dataset size and sampling (Appendix D).

Pipette-Blue preserves benign utility. Although off-policy SFT on the Pipette-Red dataset achieves low inference-time ASR in Figure 5, Table IV shows that it still incurs the utility drop identified in Remark 2 (§III-B), reducing BU on Qwen3-4B from 61.86%61.86\% to 58.76%58.76\% and on Llama-8B from 40.21%40.21\% to 29.90%29.90\%. Outcome-only RL reduces this loss but still degrades BU to 59.79%59.79\% on Qwen3-4B and 35.05%35.05\% on Llama-8B. Replacing standard adversarial training with Pipette-Blue on the same Pipette-Red dataset avoids this utility loss on both models, reaching 64.95%64.95\% BU on Qwen3-4B and 41.24%41.24\% on Llama-8B. Section V-F ablates the C1 and C2 checks and rtokr_{\mathrm{tok}} on Qwen3-4B.

V-C Robustness Against Iterative-Adaptive Attacks

We now compare the complete Pipette against training-based baselines under iterative-adaptive search (TAP and Genetic) on AgentDojo (Table V). Both searches adapt to each evaluated policy only through its attacked trajectories, using their public prompts without instructions specific to Pipette, and stop at their first success (Appendix C). Even with 4B attacker and judge LLMs, ASR on the base policies rises from 7.50%7.50\% (TAP) and 17.50%17.50\% (Genetic) on Llama-8B to 40.00%40.00\% and 70.00%70.00\% on Qwen3.6-27B, and to 50.00%50.00\% and 92.50%92.50\% on GPT-OSS-20B.

Because the base policies differ in their susceptibility to the same search, an ASR difference between two models need not reflect the effect of their defenses. We therefore compare each Pipette policy with the training-based baseline on its own model. On Llama-8B, Meta-SecAlign reaches 2.50%2.50\% ASR under TAP and 12.50%12.50\% under Genetic, compared with 0.00%0.00\% and 2.50%2.50\% for Pipette. On Qwen3.6-27B, SecOPD likewise resists TAP better than Genetic (15.00%15.00\% versus 30.00%30.00\% ASR), whereas the corresponding rates for Pipette are 2.50%2.50\% and 5.00%5.00\%. The highest ASR for Pipette is on GPT-OSS-20B, at 5.00%5.00\% under TAP and 10.00%10.00\% under Genetic. This is also the model most vulnerable to Genetic before hardening (92.50%92.50\% ASR). Thus, although the checkpoints differ in their initial vulnerability, Pipette lowers ASR under both searches relative to the baseline for each model, including GPT-OSS-20B with its native Instruction Hierarchy.

Under iterative-adaptive attacks, UA is measured on the first successful candidate or, if none succeeds, on the highest-scoring one (Appendix C). Because the agent can complete the user task and the injection task on the same trajectory, a higher UA does not by itself indicate safer task completion. On Qwen3.6-27B under Genetic, for example, SecOPD achieves 92.50%92.50\% UA at 30.00%30.00\% ASR, whereas Pipette achieves 90.00%90.00\% UA at 5.00%5.00\% ASR (Table V).

V-D Robustness Against Unseen Static Attacks

We next compare Pipette with non-training-based defenses across five unseen static attacks on AgentDojo and five on ASB (Table VI and Figure 6). On both benchmarks, their limitations appear tied to how they operate:

  • •

    Prompt boundary defenses (Spotlighting, Sandwiching) wrap observations in delimiters or repeat tut_{u} after ot′o^{\prime}_{t}. Doing so lowers ASR on plain instruction overrides such as IgnorePrev, yet is less effective when dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} spoofs chat delimiters or tool schemas in ChatInject and ToolKnow. For instance, under ChatInject on AgentDojo, Spotlighting has 45.71%45.71\% ASR on Qwen3-4B, close to the undefended base policy (46.19%46.19\%).

  • •

    External detectors and masked re-execution rely on fixed classifier boundaries (PromptGuard, PIGuard), canary prompts (DataSentinel), or masked re-execution (MELON). While PIGuard and MELON reduce average ASR to 3.33%3.33\% and 3.86%3.86\% on AgentDojo (Qwen3-4B), both have higher average ASR on ASB (Figure 6).

  • •

    System-level isolation (CaMeL) separates control flow from untrusted data by having a privileged policy write a Python-like execution plan from tut_{u} alone while a quarantined policy without tool access parses ot′o^{\prime}_{t} [60]. This prevents dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} from invoking unauthorized tools when the plan is fixed upfront, while restricting dynamic tool use (§V-E).

Despite training only on AgentDyn, Pipette has the lowest average ASR among the defenses compared under static attacks on both AgentDojo (0.48%0.48\% on Qwen3-4B and 0.43%0.43\% on Llama-8B) and ASB (0.70%0.70\% and 0.50%0.50\%, respectively). Only on AgentDojo’s ChatInject does Pipette fall outside the two lowest ASRs. PromptGuard (0.24%0.24\% on both models) and CaMeL (0.95%0.95\%) have lower ASR than Pipette (1.43%1.43\% on Qwen3-4B and 2.14%2.14\% on Llama-8B). These lower rates come at a cost: under the same attack on Qwen3-4B, UA is 16.19%16.19\% for PromptGuard and 33.81%33.81\% for CaMeL, compared with 58.10%58.10\% for Pipette (§V-E).

V-E Benign Utility and Utility Under Attack

Beyond robustness, we examine how well each defense preserves utility (R2 and R3). As shown in Table VI and Figure 6, non-training-based defenses tend to lose UA or BU, likely because they do not separate dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} from the benign data inside ot′o^{\prime}_{t}. External detectors (PromptGuard, PIGuard, DataSentinel) discard the entire flagged observation ot′o^{\prime}_{t}, removing the data needed for tut_{u} and lowering UA. Masked re-execution (MELON) and system-level isolation (CaMeL) can also block legitimate tool calls whose arguments or control flow depend on oto_{t}, which reduces UA and, in all but one case, BU. Pipette, by comparison, inspects ot′o^{\prime}_{t} in ρt+1\rho_{t+1} to ignore dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} while still extracting the benign data needed for tut_{u}.

Pipette achieves the highest BU and average static UA on AgentDojo for both models, and preserves BU on Qwen3.6-27B (92.78%92.78\% versus 93.81%93.81\% undefended; 84.54%84.54\% for SecOPD) and GPT-OSS-20B (49.48%49.48\% versus 50.52%50.52\%; Table IX). On ASB, its average UA ranks first on Llama-8B and second on Qwen3-4B, behind Sandwiching, which has higher average ASR; in all four cases, its static UA exceeds the undefended policy’s. Under iterative-adaptive attacks (Table V), its UA stays close to the base policy on GPT-OSS-20B and exceeds it on Llama-8B under TAP, while dropping on Qwen3.6-27B from 97.50%97.50\% to 87.50%87.50\% (TAP) and 90.00%90.00\% (Genetic), where SecOPD retains higher UA at higher ASR (§V-C).

V-F Component Ablation

We now ablate the components of Pipette-Blue on Qwen3-4B. Table VII compares three configurations trained for 200200 RL steps on the same Pipette-Red dataset. We measure ASR and UA under unseen ChatInject attacks and BU on clean AgentDojo tasks. Training πθ\pi_{\theta} with the trajectory-level defense reward rdefr_{\mathrm{def}} alone, without the reasoning warm-up, lowers ChatInject ASR from 46.19%46.19\% to 3.57%3.57\% and raises UA to 45.48%45.48\%, but reduces BU from 61.86%61.86\% to 59.79%59.79\%. Adding the C1 and C2 warm-up and reasoning reward lowers ASR to 2.38%2.38\% and raises UA to 56.90%56.90\%, which suggests that this inspection helps πθ\pi_{\theta} separate injected instructions from benign data inside ot−1′o^{\prime}_{t-1}. Under trajectory-level supervision alone, however, BU (60.82%60.82\%) still trails the base policy. Adding the contrastive token-level reward rtokr_{\mathrm{tok}} closes this gap, reducing ASR to 1.43%1.43\% while raising UA to 58.10%58.10\% and BU to 64.95%64.95\%.

VI Discussion and Limitations

Inference latency. All dictionary rebuilds in Pipette-Red and token-level reward queries in Pipette-Blue (Eq. 13) run offline during purple-teaming and add no runtime cost at deployment. At inference time, Pipette uses no external detector models or duplicate agent executions; its only overhead comes from generating C1 and C2 reasoning ρt\rho_{t} before tool calls ctc_{t}. As shown in Appendix A, Pipette changes the total rollout time of Qwen3-4B by −0.47-0.47 to +0.62+0.62 s and its token usage by −28%-28\% to +16%+16\% across the four suites relative to the undefended base policy, while running 1.9×1.9\times to 3.1×3.1\times faster than masked re-execution in MELON and 2.7×2.7\times to 9.5×9.5\times faster than DataSentinel.

Continuous purple-teaming. Pipette currently performs a single pass of Pipette-Red against πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} followed by Pipette-Blue, rather than alternating between red-teaming and adversarial training across multiple rounds [20]. During Pipette-Red, rebuilding the rolling dictionary 𝐃ℓ\mathbf{D}_{\ell} every MM steps keeps πϕ\pi_{\phi} exploring without retraining πθ\pi_{\theta}, since repeating an attack strategy that has entered 𝐃ℓ+1\mathbf{D}_{\ell+1} yields high ES\mathrm{ES} and near-zero rcovr_{\mathrm{cov}}. Moreover, once πθ\pi_{\theta} completes Pipette-Blue, even 250250-attempt online search achieves low ASR (Table V), which may leave a red-teaming policy initialized from πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} with too few successful rollouts to bootstrap a second round. Nevertheless, a single pass cannot reveal vulnerabilities that emerge only in the hardened πθ\pi_{\theta}, so we leave multi-round purple-teaming to future work.

Scope of the evaluation. Our iterative-adaptive evaluation is bounded by its attack budget (two search-based attacks, around 250250 attempts per task pair, a 4B attacker LLM, and 4040 task pairs), so a larger budget may achieve higher ASR. Moreover, the LLM grader behind ES\mathrm{ES} has not been validated against human labels, and we do not establish low strategy coverage as the sole cause of the gap between train-time ASR and robustness.

VII Conclusion

We find that pairing high-ASR RL-based red-teaming with standard adversarial training does not necessarily make LLM agents robust to unseen attacks. The red-teamers we study exhibit strategy-level mode collapse, and adversarial training with off-policy SFT or trajectory-level outcome rewards can reduce benign utility. To address both problems, we present Pipette, a two-stage prompt injection purple-teaming framework. Pipette-Red guides RL-based red-teaming with a rolling strategy dictionary to keep uncovering new attack strategies, and Pipette-Blue then combines task-alignment reasoning with a contrastive token-level reward to help the agent ignore injections while completing user tasks. Across four open-weight models trained on AgentDyn, Pipette achieves lower average ASR on the unseen AgentDojo and ASB benchmarks than the training-based and non-training-based baselines while preserving benign utility.

Appendix A Overhead of Pipette

Table VIII reports token usage per task (TK) and wall-clock time per rollout in seconds (TT) for Qwen3-4B on clean AgentDojo tasks. Relative to the base policy, Pipette adds the most tokens per task in Travel and Workspace, the two suites with the highest baseline token counts. We omit CaMeL from this comparison because its privileged policy can re-plan after interpreter errors and its quarantined policy can be called a variable number of times [60], making per-rollout token counts harder to compare.

Appendix B Static Attacks against Training-based Defenses

Tables IX and X complement the iterative-adaptive evaluation in §V-C by reporting the same defenses’ results on the five static attacks of each benchmark. Average ASR differs little between the separately hardened checkpoints on Llama-8B and Qwen3.6-27B. On Llama-8B, for instance, both Meta-SecAlign and Pipette keep average ASR below 1%1\%. Meta-SecAlign has the lower ASR on ChatInject (1.43%1.43\% versus 2.14%2.14\%), while Pipette has higher average UA across static attacks and higher BU on clean AgentDojo tasks. On Qwen3.6-27B, SecOPD and Pipette likewise achieve average ASR below 1%1\% on both benchmarks, with higher BU for Pipette. Comparing Pipette with the native GPT-OSS-20B gives a larger difference in attack success on AgentDojo, from 47.29%47.29\% to 2.24%2.24\% average ASR at comparable UA and BU.

Appendix C Evaluation Protocol

Benchmarks. We train both stages of Pipette and the baselines in §III on the 560560 task pairs in 𝒟tasks\mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{tasks}} from AgentDyn’s Shopping, GitHub, and Daily Life suites [39]. Because AgentDyn extends AgentDojo, the two benchmarks share general-purpose tools for email, calendars, banking, and files, and some injection tasks pursue similar goals, such as transferring money to an attacker-controlled account. Despite this overlap, their suites and individual user and injection tasks are disjoint. On AgentDojo (v1.2.2), the clean evaluation measures BU on the 9797 user tasks, each run once without injection. To evaluate the same tasks under static attacks, we use 420420 pairs, 105105 sampled per suite, covering all 9797 user tasks and 3535 injection tasks. ASB defines an attacked case as a pair of an agent and an attack tool, so we evaluate each of its five static attacks on the benchmark’s 400400 such pairs [54]. In both benchmarks, the agent policy decodes greedily at temperature 00.

Selecting the 4040 task pairs for iterative-adaptive attacks. Because TAP and Genetic each spend around 250250 rollouts of the agent policy on a single task pair (Table I), attacking all 420420 task pairs could take up to 209,160209{,}160 rollouts for every row of Table V. We therefore concentrate this budget on task pairs known to be vulnerable, namely those that static attacks already compromise on the undefended Qwen3-4B, and select 4040 of them, 1010 from each AgentDojo suite. On such a task pair, the undefended agent has been shown to read the injection and execute the injection task, which makes it a natural target for a stronger attack. ASR on this subset is thus best read as a stress test on previously compromised task pairs, not as an estimate of the rate over all 420420 task pairs. The subset is selected once and reused for every base policy and defense, so that all rows of Table V are measured on the same task pairs.

Specifically, we assign a task pair to Tier 1 if at least one static attack yields Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1 and Φtu​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})=1 on the same trajectory, i.e., the agent executes the injection task while still completing the user task, and to Tier 2 if some static attack yields Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1 but none does so with Φtu​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{u}}(\tau^{\prime})=1. Within each suite, we sort each tier by injection task ID and then by user task ID, and select 1010 task pairs from Tier 1, filling any remaining slots from Tier 2 (Table XI). This selection favors pairs on which the user task was completed under attack. UA on the selected subset is therefore not directly comparable with UA over all 420420 task pairs.

Running the iterative-adaptive attacks. Both attacks follow the configurations in Table I. The attacker LLM is huihui-ai/Huihui-Qwen3.5-4B-abliterated and the judge LLM is huihui-ai/Huihui-Qwen3-4B-Instruct-2507-abliterated, which are publicly available variants of Qwen3.5-4B and Qwen3-4B with refusal behavior removed; we choose these variants because a safety-aligned attacker LLM often declines to write injection strings. For each task pair, the attacker LLM starts from the description of tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}}, and each candidate dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} is placed at the injection position that AgentDojo defines for that pair before πθ\pi_{\theta} is rolled out in the contaminated environment. All tool calls and observations of each attacked trajectory are visible to the attacker. The judge LLM scores each failed candidate from them, and the attacker LLM proposes new candidates from the goal of tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} and its earlier candidates with their scores. TAP also discards candidates that drift from tadvt_{\mathrm{adv}} before running them and expands only the highest-scoring ones, whereas Genetic mutates a parent using other evaluated candidates as inspirations. Both attacks use the prompts of their public implementations unchanged, with no instructions specific to Pipette. Success is decided only by the injection-task checker of AgentDojo, and the search terminates at the first candidate with Φtadv​(τ′)=1\Phi_{t_{\mathrm{adv}}}(\tau^{\prime})=1 or once the attempt budget is exhausted. We report ASR as the fraction of the 4040 task pairs on which the search succeeds, so that each successful search changes ASR by 2.52.5 percentage points, and UA over the same 4040 task pairs, on the trajectory of the successful candidate or, if none succeeds, of the highest-scoring one.

Appendix D Implementation Details

Table XII lists the hyperparameters for both stages of Pipette.

Pipette-Red. We initialize the red-teaming policy πϕ\pi_{\phi} from πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} and train it against the frozen πθ0\pi_{\theta_{0}} on AgentDyn. We use Qwen3-1.7B as the LLM extractor, which writes the strategy records ψ⁡(dadv)\psi(d_{\mathrm{adv}}) and names the learned strategy primitives, Qwen3-14B as the LLM grader that computes ES\mathrm{ES} (see Appendix E for the prompts), and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B as the embedding model ℰ\mathcal{E}. We use K=32K=32 strategy primitives, chosen among {16,32,64}\{16,32,64\}, and select α\alpha at every dictionary rebuild by grid search (Table XII).

Initialization and Pipette-Blue. Before RL, we format-tune both policies with the weaker built-in static attacks of AgentDojo (e.g., Direct and SystemMsg) on AgentDyn tasks, so that πϕ\pi_{\phi} emits structured reasoning followed by dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}} and πθ\pi_{\theta} follows the C1 and C2 format; these attacks are therefore excluded from our evaluation. The reward rCoTr_{\mathrm{CoT}} comes from a Qwen3-14B judge that checks C1 and C2 at every step and averages both binary checks per trajectory.

Baselines. For RL-Hammer and PISmith, we run the code released by the respective authors with AgentDyn as the training benchmark and keep their default group sizes of 3232 and 1616, so that the batch sizes of 128128 and 6464 in Table I both correspond to four task pairs per step. For Meta-SecAlign and SecOPD, we evaluate the checkpoints released by the authors, passing tool outputs in the input role of their chat templates. Since Instruction Hierarchy is natively trained into GPT-OSS-20B, we evaluate it directly through the publicly released weights. For CaMeL, we follow its default configuration.

Compute and footprint. We ran all experiments on NVIDIA A100 GPUs with 8080 GB of memory. To limit the compute used for training and inference, we used open-weight base policies with at most 27B parameters and auxiliary models with at most 14B.

Appendix E Prompt Templates

In the prompt excerpts below, { } marks a field filled in at run time and … marks an omission. The prompts use the word “skills” for strategy records and primitives. Both privileged prefixes in Eq. 13 open the agent’s reasoning block and quote dadvd_{\mathrm{adv}}. The safe prefix z+z^{+} directs the agent to ignore the quoted text, and the unsafe prefix z−z^{-} directs it to follow the text.
